# Mercury offsite closeout — owners, cuts, launch blockers

## Frame
- Not a deck.
- Ship work, owners, cuts, blockers.
- Weekly spine = Jake.
- If discussion turns into narrative polish, cut it.

## Launch bar
- Activation works without founder handholding.
- Expansion path is visible in product, not in slides.
- Top admin pain is reduced enough that calls stop repeating the same three complaints.
- One blocker owner each.

## Activation

### Owners
- Priya: path, copy, screens.
- Jake: implementation, flag, rollout sequence.
- Anna: event definitions, success cut.

### Need by next review
- Single primary CTA: connect first source.
- Invite teammates becomes optional after first value, not before.
- Sample data only if there is no real event in the first session.
- Define activation event chain in plain English and actual events.

### Blockers
- Billing gate timing unresolved: before first real run is probably too much friction; after first value is better but needs abuse cap / usage limit.
- Event names still fuzzy; Anna needs exact handoff, Jake will not wire to vibes.
- Role setup copy still abstract; admins do not know what changes later vs now.
- Feature-flag rollout criteria are not written anywhere.

### Scope cuts
- No template gallery for v1.
- No SSO in first-run path.
- No advanced permissions setup during activation.
- No logo/upload/custom branding in first-run.

### Margin notes
- First value means connected source plus first successful action, not invited teammate.
- Stop debating empty-state illustration.
- Do not reopen the entire settings IA here.

## Expansion

### Owners
- Jake: overall.
- Priya: upgrade moments and UI.
- Anna: usage threshold sanity check and measurement.

### What stays in
- Expose upgrade trigger where usage actually hits limit.
- One clean in-app path from cap hit to plan/owner action.
- Admin sees why the workspace is constrained.
- Light copy only, no packaging essay.

### Blockers
- Mercury feature-flag rollout still ambiguous: who flips it, merge criteria, rollback note, target date.
- Usage threshold cut is noisy; need one number the team will actually use.
- Upgrade copy still split between product/admin language and billing language.

### Scope cuts
- No annual-plan flow work for launch.
- No seat-management overhaul.
- No contract-specific enterprise branching in product.
- No pricing-story work in this room.

### Margin notes
- Expansion path has to exist even if monetization details evolve later.
- If it requires sales explanation every time, it is not launch-ready.

## Admin pain

### Owners
- Jake: backend, account actions, audit surfaces.
- Priya: admin home and settings grouping.
- Anna: tag incoming issues by severity and frequency.

### Repeated pain to fix
1. Permissions / roles unclear.
2. Bulk user actions too manual.
3. No clean audit trail for who changed what.
4. Wrong person gets admin/billing noise.
5. Settings scattered across too many places.

### Blockers
- Audit-log scope unclear: what events are mandatory for launch?
- CSV/import failures still bad at telling admins what broke.
- Permission model explanation still too hand-wavey for security-conscious customers.
- Notification routing rules are not explicit enough.

### Scope cuts
- No full settings redesign.
- No granular notification matrix.
- No admin analytics dashboard.
- No custom role builder.

### Bottom line
- Fix repeated pain, not every admin complaint anyone has ever had.
- If a problem only matters after launch scale, write it down and move on.

## Cross-cutting operating rules
- Jake runs weekly from this, not Morgan.
- Morgan is pulled in only for actual scope calls / unblock.
- Devon can pressure-test logic, but not turn it into investor copy.
- Every owner comes to weekly with: what moved, what slipped, what we cut.
- Customer examples over opinions.
- Launch blockers list stays short and named.

## Open blockers to carry forward
- Billing gate timing.
- Activation instrumentation definitions.
- Mercury feature-flag rollout owner plus merge/rollback criteria.
- Admin audit-log minimum scope.

## Compact internal recap for next Mercury weekly
- Use this as operating follow-up, not a glossy launch story.
- Jake owns the weekly spine and should drive decisions against owners, cuts, and blockers.
- Priya carries activation path/copy/screens, upgrade moments/UI, and admin home/settings grouping.
- Anna carries activation definitions, success cuts, usage threshold measurement, and issue severity/frequency tagging.
- Jake carries implementation/rollout, expansion overall, backend/account actions, and audit surfaces.
- Decisions due: billing gate timing, activation event definitions, feature-flag owner/criteria/rollback/target date, and admin audit-log minimum scope.
- Do not let Monday become: can we make this story cleaner.

# Mercury activation reporting definition — May 24 correction

Owner: Anna Martinez
Audience: internal only
Source: Anna’s corrected Looker note from the May 24 review.

## Summary
The prior weekly activation cut was inflated by demo-importer / sample-import activity. Accounts that completed sample data flows were counted alongside accounts that actually connected a real source or completed a first live sync. That was too loose for activation.

## Directional cohort check

| Cohort window | Accounts created | Prior activation cut | Corrected activation cut | Inflation source |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 2023-05-08 to 2023-05-14 | 96 | 41 (42.7%) | 31 (32.3%) | 10 accounts were sample/demo-path only |
| 2023-05-15 to 2023-05-21 | 88 | 36 (40.9%) | 27 (30.7%) | 9 accounts were sample/demo-path only |

## What changed
- demo_importer and related sample flows were pulling sample_import_completed into the activation logic.
- That caused accounts to look activated before any real source was connected.
- invite_sent correlates with onboarding progress but does not by itself establish activation.

## Final mapping for Mercury activation
Count as activated within 7 days if either of these occurs:
- real_source_connected
- first_live_sync_completed

Do not count:
- sample_import_completed

Supporting evidence only, not activation by itself:
- invite_sent

## Audience limits
- This corrected cut is appropriate for internal operating use.
- Do not use this weekly cut on board or external charts.
- For board / investor retention and activation framing, stay on the sturdier cohort view rather than this weekly directional slice.

# Mercury activation empty states — June 19 decision note

Internal working-team material; not a post.

## Product decisions — Priya / Figma
- No source connected: this state does one job, get an admin to connect a real source. Primary CTA is “Connect a data source”; setup guide can be secondary.
- Do not put sample import on the no-source card in a way that reads as activation.
- If sample import remains anywhere, label it preview only. No success state, no “you’re ready,” and no green check from sample data.
- Invited member before first source: explain that the workspace exists, but an admin still needs to connect the first source. Do not tease a CTA the member cannot complete.
- First sync queued: say the source was found and the first live sync is running. No fake percentage, countdown, or precision we do not know.
- Sync failed: make the state actionable with retry plus help docs. Keep user copy product-level and do not show connector internals.
- Sample data path: remove the activated-looking success card. Sample import can help people explore, but it cannot masquerade as a live source connection.
- Do not expose internal measurement language in UI. User copy should talk about connecting a real source and seeing first live data arrive.
- CTA labels locked for now: no source “Connect a data source”; invited member “View setup guide”; queued no primary CTA; failed “Try again.”
- No celebratory success card until a real source is connected and the first live data is actually through.

## Release-readiness constraints — Marcus
- If sample import lives on the same surface, it needs separate styling and separate event names.
- Invited-member rendering must distinguish member lacks permission from org has no source yet.
- Use server role/source state for that branch; do not guess from the client session token.
- Wait for server role/source state before rendering the branch. A short loading state is better than the wrong action.
- No queued-sync percent, countdown, stepper, or ETA promise. Neutral copy like “This usually takes a couple of minutes” is acceptable.
- Need a timeout threshold for when queued becomes taking longer than usual, otherwise QA cannot test that state.
- Failed-sync release needs normalized buckets before release: auth / permissions; source unavailable / timeout; unknown / retry.
- Retry must be idempotent so double-click does not create duplicate jobs.
- No raw vendor errors in UI.
- Support contact in the failure state is unresolved; docs-only is preferred for v0.2 unless support routing is wired.
- Mobile invited-member and failure copy must be shortened before QA screenshot freeze.
- Behind the scenes, event mapping must stay aligned for engineering, QA, and Anna: invite_sent is supporting only, and sample_import_completed stays out.

## Unresolved for next review
- Whether sample data appears anywhere in v0.2 or gets cut entirely.
- Threshold for switching queued copy to taking longer than usual.
- Whether support contact appears in sync failed or only docs.
- Exact success trigger for the first pass: real_source_connected, first_live_sync_completed, or both.
- Final shortened invited-member and failure strings for mobile QA.

docs.body:
Date: July 14, 2023
Attendees: Morgan Chen, Leo Park, Jake, Priya, Marcus

Framing
- This was a release-risk and evidence readout, not a platform roadmap.
- The lens was where Mercury can still surprise us at seams, especially activation behavior depending on auth/org state and areas where dogfood evidence is thin.
- This is not an owner-split launch ledger.

## Risk 1: org-invite roles vs activation-state seam
Highest platform-seam risk is the invited-member branch because rendering depends on server role + source state, and those do not always settle at the same time.

Evidence
- Only 2 real dogfood invited-member accounts have gone end to end.
- One bug-bash pass needed refresh/re-entry before the UI settled on the expected branch.
- Confidence is still coming more from happy-path staging than repeated real dogfood coverage.

Severity / confidence
- High severity, medium confidence.

Next verification
- Run more real invited-member dogfood accounts across admin-first vs invitee-first orderings.
- Verify no path creates an activated-looking state without a real source or first live sync.
- Confirm sample data stays visually separate / preview-only and never shifts the branch into something that looks activated.
- Watch CTA selection on first load after invite accept.

Room notes
- Priya: design intent is still the four branches; no pseudo-activated middle state.
- Jake: this is release risk because it crosses auth/org state, not just copy or UI.
- Marcus: need enough evidence to know whether wrong-CTA cases are rendering issues or stale-state timing.

## Risk 2: release-readiness evidence gaps are themselves material
Leo separated implemented from proven. Some paths may be close in code but still lack enough boring real-world evidence to call them ready.

Evidence
- Invited-member branch only has 2 real dogfood accounts.
- Queued-sync retry logs are sparse even after removing fake progress / countdown behavior.
- Failed-sync screenshots are cleaner, but sample depth is still shallow.

Severity / confidence
- High severity, high confidence on the evidence gap.
- Lower confidence on how many user-facing bugs remain underneath it.

Next verification
- Targeted dogfood pass exercising each branch with saved screenshots and logs.
- Collect at least one real queue -> retry -> recovery trace for queued sync.
- Separate path unproven from path actually broken in the next pass.

## Risk 3: failed-sync cleanup still needs full verification
The failed state is close, but not fully done until every normalized bucket is verified end to end.

Evidence
- One screenshot still leaks a raw vendor string.
- Current fixes seem to cover the obvious path, but no one could confirm that auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown/retry are all equally clean.

Severity / confidence
- Medium severity, medium confidence.

Next verification
- Retest each failed bucket with captured UI.
- Confirm no raw vendor strings leak.
- Confirm retry remains idempotent.

Room notes
- Marcus said the retry action looks better but still wants proof that bucket text and UI stay normalized on every branch.
- Priya noted the warning-circle direction still seems right; the issue is verification, not revisiting the icon choice.

## Later polish vs potential blockers
- Setup-guide copy can wait unless it causes a wrong action or real confusion in the invited-member branch.
- Small-width spacing can wait unless it clips or overlaps on a supported width.
- Failed-state icon polish can wait unless it obscures state meaning.
- Priya aligned with keeping polish later as long as branch distinctions stay crisp.
- Jake said not to let a polish list turn into a second scope track before the next Mercury cycle.

## Explicit exclusions
- No abstract platform recommendations.
- No provider debate or broader auth rewrite scope.
- No SSO/admin-depth wishlist.
- Do not convert this into an owner-split launch ledger yet.

## Questions to verify next
- Can we prove invited-member rendering across real role/source-state permutations, not just the happy path?
- Do we have enough queued-sync retry evidence to say recovery is understandable without fake progress?
- Is failed-sync normalization actually complete across all buckets, or just mostly clean on the common path?
- Which gaps are real launch blockers vs thin proof on otherwise-correct behavior?
- What is the smallest next dogfood pass that materially raises confidence before we widen exposure?

# Mercury headcount checkpoint — external launch-readiness feedback checklist

Purpose: Internal product-readiness input for the Mercury headcount checkpoint before deciding any second Mercury engineering req. This is not board, investor, or B-round material.

## Feedback needed before any req decision

### 1. Source setup failure cases
- What does an external user see when the first source connection fails?
- Can they distinguish auth/permissions trouble, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown failures without us translating?
- Does recovery feel self-serve, or does it require vendor/API knowledge?

### 2. Admin handoff
- If an admin starts setup and invites an operator or teammate, does the invited person land in a sane next step?
- What happens if the invited member arrives before the first source is fully connected?
- Is the line between waiting on admin/first source and something being broken obvious?

### 3. Time to first sync
- How long does it take from first connection to first live sync in normal cases?
- If sync is queued or retried, what reassures the user that the system is working without fake progress?

### 4. Failure-state legibility
- Which failure states are understandable on first read to an external user?
- Which states still require someone from Scaffold to narrate what happened?

### 5. Confidence to try Mercury
- Clean first-run path end to end.
- One or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails.
- Proof that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle.
- Clear separation between sample/preview data and real activated state.
- Credible time-to-first-sync range, not a promise.

Decision use: Feed the req discussion only after these signals are in hand; do not convert this checklist into external collateral.

- Evergreen Bank adds enterprise-pattern substance for internal and board operating context: through Sep 4 it shows 4 admin users touching setup/settings, 12 invited members, 3 real sources connected, and successful live-sync activity on 8 distinct days.

## 2) Internal weekly diagnostics layer
The corrected weekly activation cuts are internal operating input only. They are useful for debugging admin/setup friction, sample-preview exclusions, and account-mix questions, but they should not be used in board notes, board charts, investor materials, external communication, or customer communication.

## Bounds and caveats
- Expansion remains uneven account to account: 3 accounts look meaningfully up, 3 look mostly flat, and 2 remain choppy or down.
- Evergreen is meaningful enterprise-pattern evidence, but it is still one account and not a blanket enterprise-validation claim.
- Evergreen also keeps the enterprise-readiness boundary visible: SSO timing, audit/admin depth, admin-versus-billing owner separation, and procurement packaging remain follow-up items, not Mercury v0.2 launch scope or external proof.
- This package does not prove retention is solved.
- This package does not prove expansion is solved.
- This package does not make the Mercury story external-ready.
- Do not use the weekly activation movement as a board, investor, customer, or external proof claim.

## Short version for Morgan / Devon
The September Mercury package is materially better than the May operating read on cleaner activation and admin handoff, and Evergreen adds enterprise substance. Keep the downside in the same sentence: expansion remains uneven, weekly activation movement is internal-only, and the package is not outside-ready proof.

Mercury / Evergreen procurement packet
Final — September 13, 2023
Commercial/procurement owner: Devon Hayes

1. Purpose
This packet gives Evergreen Bank a concise procurement/security review summary for the current Mercury design-partner deployment. It covers the commercial model, present login/setup scope, current admin/security posture for the bounded launch experience, and known enterprise-readiness gaps that remain outside launch scope. It is written for asynchronous procurement/security review before wider internal routing.

2. Commercial model
Mercury uses a hybrid pricing model based on monthly active developer usage, not purchased seats and not directory size.

Current bands:
- Pilot: $2,500/month platform minimum, including up to 50 monthly active developers.
- Growth: $7,500/month platform minimum, including up to 200 monthly active developers.
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers.

Counting notes:
- Monthly active developer usage is the pricing driver.
- Scaffold internal/test users do not count toward usage.
- Preview/sample-only behavior is separate from activation reporting and should not be treated as usage proof by itself.

Enterprise add-ons:
SSO, audit history for admin changes, and deeper admin controls are not included in the current launch scope. They are roadmap-dependent add-ons and would be quoted separately only after they ship.

3. Current Mercury scope
The current Mercury design-partner scope is the live bounded experience now in use:
- Clerk-backed sessions.
- Magic-link sign-in.
- Organization invites.
- Setup flow oriented around connecting a real source.
- Preview/sample data available only as preview behavior and not activating by itself.
- First live sync path in product.

Current activation definition for operating review:
- real_source_connected within 7 days; or
- first_live_sync_completed within 7 days.

Preview/sample-only behavior does not activate an account and should not be described as equivalent to real source connection or live sync completion.

Not in current launch scope:
- SSO.
- Audit history for admin changes.
- Deeper admin controls beyond the current bounded experience.
- Expanded enterprise/security packaging beyond the current design-partner flow.

4. Current login / setup experience
For the present Mercury flow, user access is handled through magic links and organization invites. Session handling is Clerk-backed. The intended path is:
1. Invited user enters through the magic-link / invite flow.
2. User lands in the Mercury workspace context.
3. User connects a real source.
4. User reaches first live sync.

Preview/sample behavior may be shown during evaluation, but preview/sample-only behavior does not activate the account.

5. Current admin / security readiness for present scope
Current readiness should be read as sufficient for the bounded design-partner experience, not as a full enterprise admin/security package.

What we can say today:
- Access is handled through the current magic-link and invite flow.
- Organization-level invitation exists in the current Mercury experience.
- The launch experience is bounded and intentionally narrower than a full enterprise rollout.
- Current product facts should be reviewed against the present scope, not against a broader enterprise-control checklist.

What this packet does not imply:
- Mercury already includes full enterprise-ready login controls.
- Current admin behavior covers all enterprise audit/control requirements.
- Later-scope items are part of the live launch package today.
- Evergreen has a bespoke roadmap path or custom roadmap commitment.

6. Known enterprise-readiness gaps
Open follow-up items surfaced in Evergreen discussions and internal review:
- SSO timing.
- Audit history for admin changes.
- Clearer separation between admin permissions and billing-owner controls.
- Stronger procurement/self-serve explanation materials that can stand on their own without Morgan or Devon live-explaining them.

These are enterprise-readiness follow-up items. They are not part of Mercury v0.2 launch scope, and they should be treated as roadmap-dependent add-ons to be quoted only after they ship.

# Kibo sitter notes — June 7, 2024 vet summary

After-Visit Summary — Kibo
Visit date: June 7, 2024
Location: Oakland
Patient: Kibo
Present with: Morgan Chen and Jamie
Visit type: Routine check

## Reason for visit
Routine check-in for Kibo before summer weather settles in.

## Summary from today
Kibo is stable overall at this routine visit.

The main items discussed were:
- Mild weight creep.
- Some fatigue in warmer weather.
- Keeping his food routine simple and measured.
- Preserving the strict no-poultry food rule.
- Shifting walks earlier on hot days.
- Planning a routine dental follow-up in fall 2024.

## Food and treats
Keep Kibo’s food boring and consistent. Do not improvise with new foods or rich treats.

Measure his regular food rather than free-pouring or adding extras. Avoid extra snacks unless Morgan and Jamie have specifically set them out for Kibo.

Hard no: Kibo must not receive poultry-based food or treats.

For Kibo, poultry includes chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, chicken meal, or similar label ingredients. If a label contains chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, chicken meal, or anything similar, do not give it to him. Skip it and ask Morgan instead of guessing.

## Warm-weather activity
Kibo has had some fatigue in warmer weather. On hot days, move walks earlier when it is cooler and keep the rest of the day lower-key rather than adding extra activity in the heat.

Kibo has mild weight creep. The plan is to keep portions measured, keep food consistent, and avoid added treats or substitutions.

## Dental follow-up
Plan a routine dental follow-up in fall 2024.

If someone else is watching Kibo, give them the food rule exactly as written:

No poultry-based treats or food for Kibo. Chicken meal counts as poultry. If a label has chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, chicken meal, or similar, skip it and ask Morgan instead of guessing.

## Plan until next routine follow-up
- Keep food simple, consistent, and measured.
- No poultry-based food or treats under any circumstances.
- Move walks earlier on hot days.
- Keep warmer days quiet if Kibo seems tired from the heat.
- Schedule routine dental follow-up for fall 2024.

# Compass prototype evidence threshold — Aug 19

Count as completed owner action only when all are present:
- named owner
- dated next action
- evidence source
- visible caveat
- completion status

Count as rejected row when:
- account note lacks source/date
- prompt sighting is too vague to act on
- row is Atlas/support context rather than Compass prompt evidence

Count as waiting row when:
- owner action is real
- status depends on live customer follow-up

Do not count as evidence:
- raw prompt sighting
- cleaner copy or better prep script alone
- Acme export timeout / Atlas support work
- customer-facing behavior change unless there is actual customer evidence

Implementation ask for Jake: rejected rows should be first-class status, not buried in notes. September readout should show completed, rejected-thin, and waiting rows separately.

docs.title: Atlas webhook delay recap — Dec 26, 2025
docs.body:
## Summary
- Holiday support rotation escalated webhook delivery delay at 9:12 AM PT.
- First observed around 8:42 AM PT.
- Delivery p95 peaked at 7 minutes 40 seconds across affected workspaces.
- Final affected count: 13 workspaces with webhook deliveries queued longer than five minutes.
- No webhook events were dropped and no data loss was found.
- Two customer support tickets asked for ETA/status; both received customer-safe updates.

## Root cause
- Retry storm on the webhook delivery queue after one source connector returned intermittent 429s.

## Response
- The team rate-limited that connector's retries.
- The team added workers to drain the queue.

## Timeline
- 8:42 AM PT: issue first observed.
- 9:12 AM PT: holiday support rotation escalated webhook delivery delay.
- 11:36 AM PT: delivery p95 returned under 25 seconds.

## Impact
- Peak p95 was 7 minutes 40 seconds.
- 13 workspaces had webhook deliveries queued longer than five minutes.
- No webhook events were dropped and no data loss was found.

## Customer messaging
- Two customer support tickets were about ETA/status rather than broken downstream state.
- Both received customer-safe delayed-but-not-dropped updates.

## Follow-ups
1. Leo owns retry-guardrail follow-up for the webhook delivery queue.
2. Sarah owns a support macro update for delayed-but-not-dropped webhook events.
3. Jake is not paged today; only involve Jake if the pattern repeats or follow-up becomes product sequencing.

Mercury / Evergreen procurement packet
Final — September 13, 2023
Commercial/procurement owner: Devon Hayes

1. Purpose
This packet gives Evergreen Bank a concise procurement/security review summary for the current Mercury design-partner deployment. It covers the commercial model, present login/setup scope, current admin/security posture for the bounded launch experience, and known enterprise-readiness gaps that remain outside launch scope. It is written for asynchronous procurement/security review before wider internal routing.

2. Commercial model
Mercury uses a hybrid pricing model based on monthly active developer usage, not purchased seats and not directory size.

Current bands:
- Pilot: $2,500/month platform minimum, including up to 50 monthly active developers.
- Growth: $7,500/month platform minimum, including up to 200 monthly active developers.
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers.

Counting notes:
- Monthly active developer usage is the pricing driver.
- Scaffold internal/test users do not count toward usage.
- Preview/sample-only behavior is separate from activation reporting and should not be treated as usage proof by itself.

Enterprise add-ons:
SSO, audit history for admin changes, and deeper admin controls are not included in the current launch scope. They are roadmap-dependent add-ons and would be quoted separately only after they ship.

3. Current Mercury scope
The current Mercury design-partner scope is the live bounded experience now in use:
- Clerk-backed sessions.
- Magic-link sign-in.
- Organization invites.
- Setup flow oriented around connecting a real source.
- Preview/sample data available only as preview behavior and not activating by itself.
- First live sync path in product.

Current activation definition for operating review:
- real_source_connected within 7 days; or
- first_live_sync_completed within 7 days.

Preview/sample-only behavior does not activate an account and should not be described as equivalent to real source connection or live sync completion.

Not in current launch scope:
- SSO.
- Audit history for admin changes.
- Deeper admin controls beyond the current bounded experience.
- Expanded enterprise/security packaging beyond the current design-partner flow.

4. Current login / setup experience
For the present Mercury flow, user access is handled through magic links and organization invites. Session handling is Clerk-backed. The intended path is:
1. Invited user enters through the magic-link / invite flow.
2. User lands in the Mercury workspace context.
3. User connects a real source.
4. User reaches first live sync.

Preview/sample behavior may be shown during evaluation, but preview/sample-only behavior does not activate the account.

5. Current admin / security readiness for present scope
Current readiness should be read as sufficient for the bounded design-partner experience, not as a full enterprise admin/security package.

What we can say today:
- Access is handled through the current magic-link and invite flow.
- Organization-level invitation exists in the current Mercury experience.
- The launch experience is bounded and intentionally narrower than a full enterprise rollout.
- Current product facts should be reviewed against the present scope, not against a broader enterprise-control checklist.

What this packet does not imply:
- Mercury already includes full enterprise-ready login controls.
- Current admin behavior covers all enterprise audit/control requirements.
- Later-scope items are part of the live launch package today.
- Evergreen has a bespoke roadmap path or custom roadmap commitment.

6. Known enterprise-readiness gaps
Open follow-up items surfaced in Evergreen discussions and internal review:
- SSO timing.
- Audit history for admin changes.
- Clearer separation between admin permissions and billing-owner controls.
- Stronger procurement/self-serve explanation materials that can stand on their own without Morgan or Devon live-explaining them.

These are enterprise-readiness follow-up items. They are not part of Mercury v0.2 launch scope, and they should be treated as roadmap-dependent add-ons to be quoted only after they ship.

Morgan Chen · Co-Founder & CEO, Scaffold

Sofia — thanks for consolidating the questions. Short written answers below.

1) October activation composition

The outside-reader definition stays unchanged: activated within 7 days means a real source was connected or first live sync completed within 7 days. Sample import / preview-only behavior does not count, and an invite sent is supporting activity only.

For the October external-share cohort, 16 of 27 reached first live sync within 7 days. An additional 3 of 27 connected a real source within 7 days but did not get through first live sync inside that same seven-day window. That 3-account gap is the full difference between 19 and 16; there is not another preview-heavy or invite-only bucket inside the activation numerator.

Shortest version: the October lift came from more accounts reaching the real-source / live-sync path in the first week; preview-only activity stayed out of the count. Operators may still see first-week behaviors such as invite accepted, sample preview viewed, or source selected, but none of those count as activation in the external-share definition.

2) Uneven expansion

Expansion is still uneven. The first-admin path is better than it was in the July/August cohorts, but broader usage still does not spread cleanly enough to call expansion solved or publish an outside expansion claim.

The main patterns are: some accounts clear setup and first live sync but stay contained to the first admin longer than we want; some broaden more slowly because trust is not established yet after first live sync; some hit admin sequencing or source-ownership confusion when the next admin/operator is added; and a smaller set need support after a failed or delayed first sync, which slows broader rollout even when activation technically happened.

The product-gap side today is mostly around admin handoff, failure-recovery clarity, and trust after first live sync. The expected design-partner side is that broader team rollout lags the initial first-admin setup even when the first path works. That is why we are comfortable speaking about activation improvement but not publishing an outside expansion claim yet. “Activated but still contained to the first admin” versus “activated with credible room to broaden” is a useful operating distinction internally, but I would not turn it into an external threshold or pseudo-metric yet.

3) Evergreen context

Evergreen is the clearest current enterprise-pattern example because the bounded Mercury flow works for a second admin group without customer-specific exceptions, not because it proves the enterprise layer is finished. In that bounded flow, Evergreen validated org invites, magic-link access, preview-only sample data, real-source connection, and first live sync.

What it surfaced more clearly are the next-phase enterprise-readiness follow-ups: SSO timing, audit history for admin changes, admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand on its own without live translation from us. Those items are clearer because of Evergreen; they are not solved by Evergreen and they are not current Mercury v0.2 claims.

I would think of Evergreen as the sharpest example of a broader enterprise pattern because the asks are recognizable rather than custom exceptions, while avoiding any implication that the pattern is already solved or broadly packaged.

4) Hybrid pricing model

The current Mercury model remains:
- Pilot: $2,500/month platform minimum including up to 50 monthly active developers
- Growth: $7,500/month platform minimum including up to 200 monthly active developers
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers
- Enterprise add-ons such as SSO, audit logs, and advanced admin controls are quoted separately only after those features ship

We map pricing to monthly active developer usage rather than purchased seats or directory size because seats and directory counts overstate value too early in this product. What matters in the current Mercury motion is how many developers are actually active in the workflow once a team gets through setup and begins real usage.

Directory size can be large before the product is actually deployed, and purchased seats push us toward selling potential ahead of actual usage. MAU is not a universal perfect metric, but it is the cleanest honest ramp measure for where Mercury is today.

For accounts that activate but expand slowly, the model deliberately avoids forcing a bigger seat commitment ahead of real usage. They can enter on the platform minimum, and the ramp in monthly active developers determines when they move up. Pricing bands map to monthly active developer usage rather than purchased seats or directory size; Scaffold/internal test users do not count; preview/sample-only behavior remains separate from activation reporting.

I would phrase the data-partner point this way: the platform minimum supports a bounded initial deployment, and MAU is what captures realized usage once the workflow broadens.

Happy to do a focused follow-up in December if useful. I would keep it through you as active diligence on the current Mercury package.
